SUBJECT:  City of Beverly Hills Electrical Resilience Action Plan

ATTACHMENTS:  1. City of Beverly Hills Electrical Resilience Action Plan

The City of Beverly Hills Electrical Resilience Action Plan (Plan), drafted by consultant
Mariko Geronimo Aydin, Lumen Energy Strategy, LLC Chief Energy Economist,
incorporates information discussed and analyzed during the Committee’s three prior
meetings. It focuses on current and future electrical issues, needs, priorities and goals.
The Plan provides the City with a framework of opportunities to improve overall electrical
reliability and provide essential community resources during emergencies or power
outages. The Plan also outlines pathways the City can incorporate to improve and
create greater electrical resiliency.

In consideration of the presented Plan, staff seeks the Committee’s recommendation on
moving forward. The Committee may adopt the measures presented, adopt with
feedback, or provide feedback and request additional information for presentation at a
future meeting.

 City of Beverly Hills: Electrical Resilience Action Plan

Executive Summary

The Mayor’s Citywide Electrical Resilience Ad Hoc Committee was formed in August 2023 with the purpose
to examine and identify potential electricity resilience improvements in the City. This report has been
prepared in response to the Committee’s desire to develop an action plan by February 2024 that includes
near-term actions implementable in 1–2 years.

The action plan is tailored to the Committee’s stated goals and priorities to (1) most importantly, improve
electricity resilience and reliability in the City, then (2) promote renewable energy and reduce the City’s
carbon footprint. Other goals of importance to the Committee include (a) electricity independence and
protections from private sector behavior, (b) access to better information on circuit performance and
investment & maintenance needs in the City, and (c) funding sources for development and renewable
energy.

Electricity customers in the City, overall, experience a higher frequency of outages compared to the
responsible utility’s system-wide average (SCE 2023). Outages in the City are caused by failures on
Southern California Edison’s (SCE) distribution system. During the 2015–2019 time period, the worst
outages occurred in the Santa Monica foothills, even absent any actual Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS)
events. In these areas, many customers experienced multiple multi-hour outages per year, with the longest
outages being 1–1.5 days. Distribution system performance in other parts of the City is mixed. Some
customers, particularly those northeast of Santa Monica Boulevard, experience a relatively high level of
outages. These outages have no clear geographic pattern or relationship to building types. Outages occur
at any, and in all, times of the year with no discernable seasonal pattern, and specific outage causes are
largely unexplained by SCE.

The City’s ability to improve resilience and reliability is complicated by growing demand for electricity, and
how that strains a system of poor electricity service and aging infrastructure. Improvements to distribution
infrastructure and related customer service would directly address the outage problems and risks faced
by the City, but this solution is entirely within the purview of SCE. So the City needs to implement a strategy
that provides key ingredients needed to (a) reduce residents’ resilience need and outage exposures, and
to (b) secure residents’ access to essential services in the event of an outage. This strategy can lead to less
outages experienced by customers, reduced outage impacts when outages do happen, and, ultimately,
more energy independence and local control over the City’s electricity infrastructure.

Near-term actions include initiatives by the City to support rapid development of energy efficiency, solar,
and energy storage resources at homes and businesses, while investing in emergency backup power
solutions at the neighborhood level to support residents for which an onsite solution is not immediately
feasible. Medium term-actions include support for development of onsite microgrids at community
facilities providing critical services (such as schools and other designated emergency shelters), and
investments in onsite microgrids to secure clean, reliable power for essential City services (such as water
treatment and other public facilities). In the long term, this new infrastructure, and our experience with
building and operating it, will serve as a gateway to the not-so-distant future of neighborhood-level
microgrids and even targeted public power.

  1
 City of Beverly Hills: Electrical Resilience Action Plan

Introduction

Overview of the MCER Ad Hoc Committee
The Mayor’s Citywide Electrical Resilience Ad Hoc Committee (MCER Ad Hoc Committee, or Committee)
was formed in August 2023 with the purpose to examine and identify potential electricity resilience
improvements. A key motivation for Committee formation stems from widespread dissatisfaction with the
quality of electricity service in the City, and, as electricity demand grows, concerns over ongoing and
growing dependence on poorly-performing distribution infrastructure. The Committee’s term is expected
to extend through at least summer 2025 or until near-term actions can be implemented.

Definition of Electrical Resilience
The power industry has no standard definition of resilience, but themes include:

  •  The hazard/event is distinguished from the system that needs to be resilient against it;
  •  The resilience hazard/event is uncontrollable and disruptive to the system in question;
  •  A resilient system withstands, absorbs, recovers from, and adapts to disruptions;
  •  The system provides some critical function that must be defined and prioritized;
  o What are the critical facilities, other sites providing critical services, high-priority loads?
  •  Each community has its own unique risks, risk tolerances, and risk management preferences;
  defining the following is a key step to effective resilience planning:
  o What are the drivers (hazards) of service interruptions; where are the failure points?
  o What types of facilities, sites, and/or loads must be prioritized and protected?
  o Given costs of solutions, how much resilience or outage protection is optimal?

As the City considers its options to improve electricity resilience, to minimize confusion and
misunderstanding, the establishment of clear, precise and effective definitions for key terms is essential.
For the purposes of the MCER Ad Hoc Committee, electricity resilience is defined as the ability to
withstand, reduce, and recover from electricity service interruptions during a major event that leads to
significant or cascading failures of the grid.

This is distinct from, but related to, electricity reliability, which we define as the ability of the grid to deliver
electricity within certain criteria and on average considering a range of possible grid conditions and
contingencies.

Committee Goals and Priorities
The Committee aims to develop a resilience action plan by February 2024 and to implement near-term
actions by summer 2025.

The Committee also emphasized the need to expedite selection of a subset of resource solutions that can
be implemented as quickly as possible to build a record of success and build momentum towards
additional future resilience investments. This report includes recommendations on specific resource
solutions that can be implemented relatively quickly.

As part of the inaugural Committee meeting, on August 30, 2023, committee members discussed the need
to establish clear goals and priorities. In follow-up to that meeting each Committee member completed a
survey indicating their preferences. Results are shown in Figure 1.

Electricity resilience and reliability are the highest priorities to the Committee, with renewable energy and
reduction of carbon footprint also very important. Bill savings and various types of power sales to the

Results confirm that clean energy development is a high priority for the City, but not at the expense of
resilience and reliability. This indicates that non-renewable energy sources such as diesel backup
generation could be an option, perhaps in emergency situations or for sites where residences and
businesses are particularly vulnerable in an outage situation and where installation of solar and/or storage
is not feasible.

Lower priority rankings on bill savings and power sales to the grid indicate that the City’s target resource
sizes and configurations should be tailored to the level of outage mitigation needed. For example, this
suggests that it would not be a priority for the City to target onsite solar + storage in a microgrid
configuration at sites where 10-hour backup power is sufficient.

Other goals of importance to the Committee include (a) electricity independence and protections from
private sector behavior, (b) access to better information on circuit performance and investment &
maintenance needs in the City, and (c) funding sources for development and renewable energy.

Approach to Action Plan Development
The Committee held three meetings in 2023 to guide development of a resilience action plan.

In the first meeting, held on August 30, 2023, the Committee reviewed key information on the City’s
distribution grid and outage patterns, relationship to the broader bulk grid, microgrid attributes, and
resilience concepts. Committee members discussed their concerns and perspectives on the City’s
resilience problem, and their goals and priorities.

  3
 City of Beverly Hills: Electrical Resilience Action Plan

In the second meeting, held on September 27, 2023, the Committee established its goals and priorities,
reviewed detailed data on historical distribution circuit-level outages, discussed the interdependence of
resilience solutions with the City’s emergency management activities, and further discussed a plan to
initiate an onsite resilience audit program.

In the third meeting, held on November 1, 2023, the Committee reviewed industry information and
lessons learned on resilience strategies and resource solutions applicable to the City, heard from SCE on
their available funding and tariff options for resilience solutions, and heard from a representative of the
Pali Microgrid on their experiences. Discussion focused on identifying resilience solutions realistically
implementable in the near term versus longer-term, and what utility, state, and federal support is
available.

  4
 City of Beverly Hills: Electrical Resilience Action Plan

Electricity Service in the City

In the electricity grid electricity flows from generators “upstream” to customers “downstream.” The U.S.
grid is designed such that electricity mostly follows a path of least resistance. The transmission system,
which is the bulk “highway” delivery system, is built as a mesh for redundancy. So, if a transmission wire
is out of service, then electricity can usually find another way to its destination. The distribution system,
however, is built radially, like local roads. So if a distribution wire is out of service, then usually electricity
service to all downstream customers is interrupted.

The City’s Electricity Grid
As of 2023, 48 distribution circuits serve the City of Beverly Hills, shown in Figure 2. These circuits connect
to 5 substations upstream, towards the transmission system, with most circuits connecting to the Beverly
substation in the downtown area. Through the Flats northwest of Santa Monica Boulevard and into the
Santa Monica foothills (“Hills”), 11 circuits are located in a Tier 2 High Fire Threat District (HFTD) and
designated as Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) circuits. This is the second-highest type of wildfire threat
area in the state, with Tier 3 being the highest. No actual outages due to PSPS have been implemented on
these circuits to date.

 City of Beverly Hills: Electrical Resilience Action Plan

Observed Outage Problem and Grid Failure Points
To better understand the City’s outage patterns and problem areas a range of publicly available reports
and data were reviewed, including SCE’s Annual Electricity Reliability Reports, the utility’s periodic Circuit
Reliability Reviews presented to the City, detailed circuit-level outage data for the 5-year period 2015–
2019 provided by SCE in its Wildfire Mitigation Plans, additional information on circuit characteristics
provided as part of SCE’s Wildfire Mitigation Plans and its distributed energy resources planning studies.

Overall, outages occur at all times of the year, mostly with no discernable seasonal pattern. 70–80% of
outages are driven by equipment failures or causes unknown to SCE.

Circuit locations and total daily circuit-outage hours for a subset of 35 circuits serving the City indicate
that, during the 2015–2019 time period, the worst outages occurred in the Hills even absent any actual
Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) events—and even for circuits that are not PSPS circuits. Most circuits
in the Hills are partially overhead, connect to the Beverly substation, and are located in the elevated
wildfire risk area. Many customers in the Hills experienced multiple multi-hour outages per year, with the
longest outages being 1–1.5 days. Outages occur at any, and in all, times of the year with no discernable
seasonal pattern, with some exceptions as the Committee has indicated SCE’s more recent work on the
Playboy circuit in the northeast corner of the City revealed water intrusion issues from rain and flooding.
Figure 4 provides an example of the outage time profile in the Hills, using outage data for the Hilton circuit.

In its quarterly Wildfire Mitigation Plan report for Q2 2023, SCE indicates that customers on the Hilton
(Figure 4) and Coldwater circuits have relatively higher vulnerability to both wildfires and PSPS due to
customers designated as (but not limited to) Critical Care, Disabled, Medical Baseline, Low Income, Limited
English, Pregnant, and Children. This relatively high vulnerability is in comparison to other PSPS circuits in
the City and compared to average vulnerabilities across all PSPS circuits in the SCE system. As of Q2 2023,

  7
 City of Beverly Hills: Electrical Resilience Action Plan

SCE data indicate the Playboy circuit has the highest PSPS risk in the City, with risk defined as a function of
PSPS likelihood and consequence. The Playboy circuit’s PSPS risk is driven by the relatively high number of
customers on that circuit, and despite the circuit being largely undergrounded.

According to SCE data, some circuits located partially or entirely in the Hills, apparently do not currently
face PSPS risk, but customers still may face the elevated risk of wildfires coming to these portions of the
grid and to their properties. The Harratt circuit, for example, is not subject to PSPS because that line is
100% undergrounded, but it is fully located in the Trousdale area of the Hills and so both the line and its
residential customers are still at an elevated risk for wildfire spread and associated damage. SCE upgraded
the circuit to 16 kv in March of 2023.

The best-performing circuits in the 2015–2019 period are four circuits located in the Flats with no circuit
portions in the Hills. It should be noted that most of the circuits in the Hills described above are connected
to the Beverly substation in the downtown area and so have portions coming up through the Flats to the
Hills. This means that, aside from the four relatively well-performing circuits, many customers in the Flats,
such as those served by the Hilton circuit, suffer from the same relatively poor circuit performance as
customers in the Hills although they do not face the same wildfire risks.

Several circuits are clustered in the downtown area, serving commercial customers. Most are 100%
undergrounded and all connect to the nearby Beverly substation. Many of these customers experience a
1–2 multi-hour (1–4 hour) and/or 1 extended (10-20 hour) outage every other year.

Circuit performance in other parts of the city southeast of Santa Monica Boulevard is mixed. Customers
experience relatively low, moderate, elevated, or high outages depending on the circuit and with no clear
geographic pattern or relationship to building types. Most customers experience relatively low or
moderate outages, similar to downtown customers: 1–2 multi-hour (1–4 hour) and/or 1 extended (10-20
hour) outage every other year.

Resilience Planning Areas

It is clear that not all residents and businesses in the City have the same outage experiences,
vulnerabilities, and resilience needs, and consequently that there is unlikely to be a one-size-fits-all
solution.

Building type presents both constraints and opportunities for resilience solutions. High-rise and many
types of commercial buildings, for example, are typically not well suited for solar panels due to small
rooftop or other space to host PV panels relative to the building’s electricity demand levels—but they may
be able to install a significant amount of energy storage. As shown in the City’s Safety Element (Figure 3,
above), buildings in the Flats and Hills are primarily single-family homes; commercial buildings are
concentrated downtown and along major roadways, and homes southeast of Santa Monica Boulevard are
a mix of multi-family homes and single-family homes.

Looking at outage characteristics and building types, the City’s electricity resilience strategies should
consider the five distinct resilience planning areas and target populations as outlined in

Key Hazards to Electricity and Other Essential Services
As described above, actual outages in the City are driven by failures on the distribution system, with the
underlying cause or hazard unexplained. To achieve resilience to a range of potential future hazards, it is
essential that the City’s electrical resilience strategy is integrated with the City’s Safety Element and
Emergency Operations Plan.

The City’s Safety Element, Emergency Operations Plan, and Hazard Mitigation Plan all describe a number
of potential hazards to the City and its communities, shown in Figure 6. Geological fault lines run roughly
East-West through the middle of the City. Areas along the northern (upper Hills), southern, and eastern
perimeter of the city are in liquefaction zones, and many parts of the Hills are in landslide zones. Most of
the City downslope from the Hills lies within an extremely high inundation hazard area. In the event of a
natural disaster, entire neighborhoods may need to evacuate or may be displaced.

It is also essential to develop an electricity resilience strategy that integrates insights from the City’s Safety
Element and Emergency Operations Plan by considering how backup power, solar + storage installations,
onsite microgrids, and other local electricity resources would perform and support community needs in
the event of a natural disaster or other emergency situation.

The City has identified a number of critical facilities located at the neighborhood level that will likely play
a critical role in providing services and resources during emergencies. Securing power at sites that provide
critical services to the community in the event of an emergency can also support community members
who are vulnerable during less extreme or day-to-day “blue sky” outages. A comprehensive resilience
strategy will integrate these two levels of resilience solutions, with the understanding that installation of
solar, storage, or solar + storage on every home is not the goal and not realistic—nor would it be sufficient
to ensure people have access to critical services in an emergency.

Examples from the State’s Self-Generation Incentive program of mostly non-residential sites providing
critical services include: police stations; fire stations; emergency response providers; emergency
operations centers; 911 call centers; medical facilities including hospitals, skilled nursing facilities, nursing
homes, blood banks, health care facilities, dialysis centers and hospice facilities; public and private gas,
electric, water, wastewater or flood control facilities; jails and prisons; cooling centers; homeless shelters;
neighborhood grocery stores, corner stores, markets and supermarkets; independent living centers; and
food banks.

Other types of facilities that provide critical services to consider include schools, gas stations and electric
vehicle chargers.

  11
 City of Beverly Hills: Electrical Resilience Action Plan

Resilience Resources, Examples, and Opportunities

Prior Initiatives and Existing Resources in the City
Since 2008 the City of Beverly Hills has developed several initiatives to reduce the City’s energy burden,
promote clean and sustainable energy, and improve energy independence and local control.

The City has supported homes and businesses by making improvements to solar permitting and
developing solar installation guidelines. The City also invested in solar rooftops on several City-owned
properties, including the Foothill Road office building, library, police facility, and Civic Center garage.

In around 2012, the City made a number of investments in HVAC and lighting energy efficiency that
leveraged financing from SCE’s former Special Benefit Management Affiliates (MAP) program. Through
that program, the City was able to improve energy efficiency across 21 City facilities, including garages,
parks, City Hall, a police facility, the library, and the Public Works building.

In 2019 the City joined the Clean Power Alliance in order to give residents and businesses more options to
secure clean, renewable power at competitive rates. Although full electricity municipalization is not
achievable at this time, the City continues to seek opportunities for more options and independence in its
electricity supply.

Additional Potential Resilience Resources and Strategies
  What is the “Ideal” Resource Solution?

For the City of Beverly Hills, specifically, upgrades to the distribution circuits and better tracking and
communication of outage causes and remedies would go a long way to address resilience and reliability
concerns in the City. Absent these actions by SCE, resources at the building, neighborhood, and city level
will need to be carefully considered.

Industry examples of the ideal energy-resilient communities often point to new housing developments,
where a comprehensive resilience strategy can be fully integrated with the design of the built environment
and community infrastructure from day one. Although it is unrealistic for an existing community like
Beverly Hills to retrofit its core architecture to mimic a new-build community, these case studies provide
a good benchmark for the key elements of a good resilience strategy.

Shadow Mountain, shown in Figure 7, is a new housing development located in Menifee, California. Two
communities within Shadow Mountain (Durango and Oak Shade communities), including over 200 homes,
are developed specifically to enhance electricity service reliability and resilience. The development is SCE
grid-connected, and it includes a community-level microgrid, a community battery energy storage system
(BESS), home efficiency and smart home advancements, rooftop solar installations, and individual home
battery energy storage systems.

Communities like this illustrate the need for a multi-layered resilience action plan, which targets resilience
improvements in homes and individual buildings and at the neighborhood level. This approach builds
multiple layers of redundancy to protect against outages, which is especially important for the most

Common industry solutions, currently in-practice and relevant to the City include:

  •  Storage and other backup power solutions for areas experiencing relatively moderate or elevated
  outages and needing improved year-round reliability;
  •  Continued solar and efficiency initiatives to moderate demand growth even in areas with relatively
  good circuit performance;
  •  Solar + storage onsite microgrid solutions in areas of elevated wildfire risk and relatively poor
  circuit performance; and
  •  Mobile emergency backup power and/or microgrid options at the neighborhood level to secure
  power at critical sites or clusters of critical sites during both outages and greater emergencies.

  Energy Efficiency

Through reduction in energy use, energy efficiency (EE) can yield benefits of avoided energy costs and any
associated pollutant emissions, and a reduced energy need and impacts during power system
interruptions and emergencies. Prior City efforts include identification of HVAC, lighting, and equipment
efficiency upgrades at several City facilities and parking structures. The costs of incremental energy
efficiency can be highly building-specific, depending on building type and how efficient the building
already is. Cost-effective energy efficiency can be identified through an energy audit or EE potential study.

  Geothermal

The prospect of new geothermal energy was raised in an earlier Committee meeting. New geothermal
power plants were recently procured in California, for the first time in a decade (Roth 2020). Locations
with the most geothermal potential include The Geysers area (Sonoma, Lake, and Mendocino counties),
Salton Sea (Imperial County), Coso Hot Springs (Inyo County), and Mammoth Lakes (Mono County) (CEC
2023).

Another type of geothermal resource—geothermal, or ground-source, heat pump—is a mature
technology more widely available to homes and businesses across the state. Heat pumps are sometimes
described as a type of energy efficiency. Ground-source heat pumps use subsurface ground temperatures
to provide high-efficiency heating and cooling to buildings. They significantly reduce building energy
consumption. In the case of a grid outage heat pumps must be paired with backup power or in a microgrid
configuration in order to function. Due to its efficiency benefit, and to the extent the heat pump uses clean
electricity or onsite clean energy, heat pumps can also promote the use of clean energy.

Ground-source heat pumps are more expensive than air-source heat pumps, but they may be installed as
hybrid ground/air systems for cost savings while retaining much of the efficiency advantages.

The key feature is a series of buried pipes filled with water or coolant. These are needed for temperature
exchange with the ground. If installed horizontal to the ground, a mid-sized home installation would
require burying pipes about 10 feet deep across a 7,500 square foot area. Vertical installations use less
land but are more costly. They require drilling boreholes several hundred feet into the ground and a
geological survey.

Geothermal heat pump installations on an existing home have a relatively high up-front cost, on the order
of $30,000 for a mid-sized home, followed by significant energy savings. The DOE estimates the payback
period at 5–10 years. Home installations of geothermal heat pumps are eligible through 2032 for the
Federal Residential Clean Energy Credit and may qualify for other state or utility rebates.

  Onsite Solar PV

Solar PV panels are a mature technology that is widely used by homes and businesses in California. As of
the end of 2023, Los Angeles County includes about 118,000 customer-sited installations, mostly on
residential buildings (both in terms of total MW and number of installations) (Energy Solutions 2023).
Solar PV installations promote direct self-consumption of renewable energy, and, depending on sizing and
site conditions, may also send clean electricity into the broader grid.

Solar PV panels alone cannot mitigate electricity service interruptions to customers. To do so, they must
be paired with energy storage and configured to electrically island a home in the case of a grid outage.
Solar PV panels require ample space, are typically installed on rooftops, and perform best when they are
angled to capture as much solar insolation as possible, unobstructed by trees, adjacent buildings, and
sediment.

Recent self-reported costs to install solar PV in LA County homes are about $5 per watt (AC) (Energy
Solutions 2023), or about $35,000 for a 7 kW system. Solar PV installations are incentivized through
several mechanisms, including retail electricity tariffs that pay customers for excess generation exported
to the grid, the State’s Self-Generation Incentive Program, and Federal tax credits.

  Onsite Energy Storage

Lithium-ion battery energy storage is now a mature technology that is widely available for installation at
homes and businesses. Los Angeles County includes about 7,600 customer-sited installations, mostly on
residential buildings (both in terms of total MW and number of installations) (Energy Solutions 2023).

Depending on configuration and sizing relative to customer electricity demands, the ability of energy
storage to mitigate electricity service interruptions can range from a few hours of backup power (typically
as standalone storage) to multiple days of support (typically in a microgrid configuration with solar PV).

Nearly all energy storage installed in homes is paired with solar PV where it can help manage electricity
bills by charging during the day when solar generation is abundant and retail rates are low, and by
discharging in the evening as solar generation declines and retail rates peak. Standalone energy storage is
not currently economical for most homes and is not widely in use compared to solar plus storage
installations. For commercial buildings subject to peak demand charges, however, standalone energy
storage can be economical to manage those charges by discharging to mitigate peak demand during the
day, then charging slowly in the evening or nighttime. The use of thermal energy storage in commercial
buildings subject to demand charges is also in practice since they can be connected directly to HVAC
systems and help reduce HVAC peak demands during the day.

Lithium-ion batteries require relatively small installation space, but there are many important safety
considerations to placement, installation, and use. Thermal energy storage systems require more space to
accommodate equipment such as tanks or tubes.

Recent self-reported costs to install batteries in LA County homes are about $6 per watt (AC) (Energy
Solutions 2023), or about $30,000 for a 5 kW system. Installation of solar plus storage can realize several
thousand dollars in cost savings through shared inverters and synergies in “soft” (non-hardware) costs. As
with solar PV, energy storage is incentivized through several mechanisms, including retail electricity tariffs
that compensate a storage charge/discharge schedule that is advantageous to the grid, the State’s Self-
Generation Incentive Program, and Federal tax credits.

  Microgrids

A microgrid is a system of local electricity loads (demand), resources, wires, control equipment, and other
elements, that work together as a mini-grid. Grid-tied microgrids can toggle between (macro) grid mode
and (isolated) island mode seamlessly while serving its loads.

Microgrids are capable of mitigating (macro) grid outages for long periods of time. Resources may include
fossil-fired resources (e.g., diesel generators) and/or renewable resources paired with batteries.

Microgrids require special equipment to detect grid outages, seamlessly transition in and out of island
mode, form a grid, and reliably meet internal loads. The electrical scope of a microgrid is customizable and
can be developed to support a single building, a group of buildings, a neighborhood, or an entire
distribution circuit. However, a microgrid’s ability to mitigate outages depends on the condition and
configuration of equipment (including wires) within the microgrid’s scope, both of which can be major cost
and logistical barriers to microgrid development beyond single buildings and campuses. Examples of actual
installed larger-scale microgrids are either serving “grid-edge” communities for which the primary
motivation for the microgrid is service interruption upstream from the distribution substation, serving

other similar unique community situations, or new housing developments for which the microgrid can be
included in land and building development plans—none of which are applicable to the City.

  Other Power Backup Solutions

Stationary and mobile diesel backup generators are crucial resources needed to support local resilience
and to secure power supply at critical sites such as hospitals. They are a mature technology, relatively low
initial investment cost, flexible, and scalable. Key tradeoffs include polluting emissions impacts and
uncertainties in fuel supply or fuel costs during an emergency.

Mobile storage and solar plus storage solutions have also emerged in the industry. One example is a set of
mobile solar plus storage trailers used for emergency services after 2021 Hurricane Ida and to power crisis
response centers (St. John 2023).

  Notable Resource Strategies Relevant to the City

Resilience resource strategies at the city level are multi-layered and must include a portfolio of different
types of resources that work together to address the City’s many dimensions of resilience and reliability
needs. Examples of new development resilient communities, in which resilience can be built directly into
the community design, provide some indication of the complexity of resilience infrastructure and
activities. These types of communities are designed to withstand electricity service at multiple failure
points, for example, by being grid-connected, with a backstop of community-level microgrid capability
including solar and storage resources, and another backstop with individual homes and buildings equipped
with solar and storage resources.

In an already-built environment like the City, resilience planning and investments must be retrofit to
existing structures to the extent feasible and cost-effective. With this in mind, and with a layered approach,
several industry examples of the above-described resources in use may be relevant to the City and its
resilience and reliability needs.

Energy efficiency, where cost-effective across the City, will not fully mitigate outage impacts but will
reduce energy and resilience needs and, in doing so, provide opportunities for cost savings. Beyond
lighting and equipment efficiency upgrades, heat pumps (whether ground-source or air-source) may be of
interest to people in the City as another efficiency opportunity.

Residential standalone solar, in areas where circuit reliability is good with relatively low outage risk,
promotes clean energy and energy independence, and banks for a future in which neighborhood
microgrids are possible. The Pali Microgrid currently in early development in the Pacific Palisades, for
example, follows a strategy to negotiate bulk purchases of rooftop solar and energy storage that would
then be connected into a larger microgrid system. This microgrid is “expected to be one of the first
community microgrids in the US installed in an established residential community” (Wood 2022).

Residential solar plus storage, particularly in the Hills and on circuits with an elevated level of outages
southeast of Santa Monica Boulevard In emergencies, helps households withstand longer-duration
outages lasting days, and promotes clean energy and energy independence. Solar plus storage can also
serve critical loads in people’s homes over a long time period during an emergency, reducing burden on
the City’s emergency response teams. In the example of Babcock Ranch in Florida, the community was not

only able to maintain its own critical services, but it provided relief to surrounding communities destroyed
by Hurricane Ian in 2022 (Dean 2022).

Commercial standalone storage, where space for solar PV panels may not be available, can help mitigate
the relatively short-duration outages experienced by those customers (if backup power is provided by
batteries). It can also help customers manage day-to-day peak demands on the distribution system
monetizable as reduction in demand charges, and this helps to defer needs for SCE to upgrade the
distribution system. As an example, the Beverly Hilton and Waldorf Astoria Beverly Hills hotels recently
announced procurements of thermal energy storage systems that would significantly reduce the buildings’
air conditioning loads (Richardson 2023).

Single-site microgrids, at critical facilities and community centers can provide support for people
experiencing outages at their homes. In addition to City facilities such as fire stations and the library,
schools and colleges are trusted community hubs that can help provide basic services during an extended
outage or emergency. As an example (though it is a multi-building example), the Santa Rosa Jr. college in
Sonoma County developed a microgrid that improves resilience to PSPS and emergencies, reduces peak
demand charges, and synergizes EE investments and migration to solar power and away from backup
diesel generators (Liebman et al. 2023).

Federal, State, and Utility Funding Sources
Federal, state, and local governments offer funding in the form of grants, tax credits and other incentives
to eligible parties meeting certain criteria. The federal government provides individuals several tax credits
and incentives for energy efficiency upgrades. Utility companies offer incentives and rebates to their
customers. For example, Southern California Edison (SCE) offers online guided home efficiency tools and
rebates for installing qualified energy-efficient products, as well as information regarding third-party
programs and how they may be able to assist in energy conservation and lowering energy costs; The
federal government allows for tax credits that reduce tax liability. Tax credits, rebates and incentives are
available for individuals and government entities. While not an exhaustive list, some general sources are
listed in the following sections.

  Tax Incentives

  Residential Federal Incentives

As part of the Inflation Reduction Act Tax Credits, the Residential Clean Energy Credit and the Federal
Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit cover improvements to the main home of homeowners and
renters (certain improvements only) of 30% of the cost for qualified energy efficiency improvements,
residential energy property expenses and home energy audits, available until 2035. Individuals can claim
either the Residential Clean Energy Credit or the Federal Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit. A
few examples of credits include:

  •  Expenses covering solar panels, solar water heaters, fuel cells and battery storage.
  •  The home energy audit tax credit allows a tax credit of $150 for a home energy audit for an audit
  conducted by a home energy auditor resulting in a written report and inspection, among other
  qualifiers (additional requirements for 2024).

  •  The Building Envelope Components credit covers energy-efficient improvements and is available
  for door and window replacements and equals $250 per door, for a total of $500 and $600 for
  exterior windows and skylights meeting efficiency standards.
  •  Home improvements including doors, insulation, windows and skylights.

The amount of credit for Residential Clean Energy Credit through 2032 is 30% of the costs of new, qualified

Restrictions apply – some public utility subsidies, rebates and State incentives may need to be subtracted
if they are deemed purchase-price adjustments and use of dwelling is a factor (main home, business use
of home, landlord, etc.).

The amount of credit for Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit through 2032 is 30% of the total
improvement expenses in the year of installation of certain qualified expenses. From 2023, through 2032,
the credit is 30% of qualified expenses with a maximum of $1,200.

The U.S. Department of Energy, Office of State and Community Energy Programs (SCEP) Elective Pay – Cash
for Clean Energy: This program gives local governments the opportunity to receive cash payments from
the federal government for eligible clean energy investments following the completion of certain projects.
A 30% tax credit allows entities to receive 30% of the project investment cost back in a cash payment.
Projects could include solar, EV chargers, clean electricity, storage, microgrids, and other energy projects
covered under the Inflation Reduction Act clean energy tax credits. The City could benefit from this credit,
after completing pre-filing registration, by completing a federal tax return and making an elective payment
election on qualifying clean energy investments.

  Residential State Incentives

California state property tax exemptions for qualifying solar energy systems will exempt the added value
of a solar system from property taxes through January 1, 2025.

  Rebate Incentives

Rebate incentives are generally in the form of a partial return of a payment or credit on a purchase, given
to encourage purchase of a product or service. Rebate incentives can be a factor in terms of funding to
reduce the cost for individuals and businesses to use alternative energy resources. Examples of these
types of rebates are below.

  Residential Federal Rebates

The U.S. Department of Energy has a number of offerings. Among several programs available, funding is
set aside for home energy efficiency and electrification projects to encourage clean energy, decrease
greenhouse gases, and increase energy efficiency. The Office of State and Community Energy Programs
(SCEP) works with state and local organizations to significantly accelerate the deployment of clean energy
technologies, through strategies involving a wide range of stakeholders. Administered by the States, the

The U.S. Department of Energy Grid Resilience and Innovation Partnerships (GRIP) Program for Fiscal Years

  Utility Provider Residential Rebates

California’s SGIP – Self Generation Incentive Program, operated by the California Public Utilities
Commission and administered by utility companies, provides rebates for residential and non-residential
customers who install and use energy storage systems. The SGIP rebate works as a reimbursement after
the project is installed and applies to both the equipment and installation cost of a battery storage project.
As customers of Southern California Edison (SCE), Beverly Hills residents in Tier 2 or 3 High Fire Threat
Districts (north of Sunset) or those who have experienced two or more utility Public Safety Power Shut-
offs (PSPS’s), and are medically vulnerable (enrolled in/eligible for a Medical Baseline Program or provided
SCE notice of a serious illness/life-threatening condition in the event of a power failure) can participate in
SCE’s self-generation incentive program, potentially covering a significant portion of the cost to install self-
generating energy storage systems. For those who do not qualify for the higher rebates, a General Market
Rebate for approximately 25% of the cost of an average system is available through solar providers.

Net Energy Metering (NEM) Credit incentives for solar energy allow homeowners on the Time-of-Use rate
to receive time-of-use credits for the excess electricity their solar panels generate and export to the grid.
SCE’s NEM program allows grid-connected customers to receive a credit for surplus electricity their system
sends to the grid.

Administered by various entities, Golden State Rebates are available to SCE customers. These rebates (in-
store/online redeemable coupons) cover energy efficient products such as room air conditioners ($15
rebate), smart thermostats ($75 rebate) and water heaters (up to $900 rebate for heat pump water heaters
and up to $75 rebate for gas tank water heaters).

assist in lowering initial costs. Both State and Federal incentives are available to potential EV users.

Several channels are within the City’s reach to collect detailed circuit and/or customer outage data from
SCE. Pursuant to CPUC Decision 16-01-008, the utilities are “required… to make reliability data available
to the public upon request” (CPUC n.d.). Detailed outage data and information on wildfire-related are
available to stakeholders through California Wildfire Safety Advisory Board proceedings, with publicly-
available information posted on the utilities’ websites. California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC)
proceedings related to climate adaptation and distribution system planning also contain detailed data and
information from the utilities on grid vulnerabilities and planned investments—often at the distribution
circuit and substation level. Alternatively, third party vendors like poweroutage.us may provide a data
collection and data processing service.

  Action (NEAR TERM): Increase regulatory pressure to SCE to significantly improve its
  investigations and reporting of outage causes.

A large share of distribution outages are driven by equipment failures or causes unknown to SCE. This
creates a major knowledge gap as the City seeks to improve the resilience and reliability of its electricity
supply. City representation as a stakeholder in CPUC proceedings related to distribution reliability and
planning provides a channel for the City to submit formal stakeholder comments, data requests, and
protests.

Actions to Reduce Electricity Resilience Needs and Outage Exposures
Through a variety of knowledge-building initiatives and continued permitting improvements, the City has
an important role in facilitating development of onsite energy efficiency and outage mitigation resources
on homes and businesses. These private investments can help reduce onsite electricity resilience needs
and outage exposures, but, as with many types of building upgrades, interested (or potentially interested)
electricity customers may face a variety of information and logistical barriers.

  Action (NEAR TERM): Facilitate onsite energy resilience audits for interested residents
  and small businesses.

As with a traditional home energy audit, resilience-focused audit can help electricity customers better
understand their building-specific vulnerabilities and realistic investment opportunities. They can get
advice from a qualified professional without sales pressure from developers. At the same time, the City
can collect valuable information on customer concerns, interests, and most suitable resource solutions,
which can be used to further refine and direct the City’s resilience strategy.

  24
 City of Beverly Hills: Electrical Resilience Action Plan

  Action (NEAR TERM): Build a resilience knowledge center on the City’s website,
  updated regularly.

This knowledge center can help residents and small businesses better understand the suite of resource
options available to them, the pros and cons of each, and available funding sources. Information-sharing
can also be triggered by certain types of permit applications, such as a fact sheet about the pros and cons
of rooftop solar when a resident applies for a roofing permit.

  Action (NEAR TERM): Provide additional permitting support for residents and
  businesses who seek or may be interested in installing resilience resources such as
  solar, energy storage, and energy efficiency.

Information-sharing can also be triggered by certain types of permit applications, such as a fact sheet
about the pros and cons of rooftop solar when a resident applies for a roofing permit. Expedited electrical
and solar permits and inspections, along with clear guidelines on safe installation, can also facilitate more
rapid development of resilient energy infrastructure.

  Action (MID TERM): Negotiate bulk customer-sited solar and/or energy storage
  purchases for interested residents and small businesses.

If the resilience audits indicate sufficient interest, consider screening developers and negotiating a bulk
discount rather than having each resident and small business go through this process individually. Bulk
purchases can create true cost savings, for both customers and developers since developers can reduce
marketing cost and coordinate multiple installations at once.

  Action (LONG TERM): Pilot a neighborhood-level microgrid.

Neighborhood-level microgrids are installed on the distribution system but much closer to the customer
than a substation-level microgrid. These types of microgrids have the advantage of mitigating distribution-
level outages and economies of scale in neighborhood-level resources (e.g., neighborhood energy storage
rather than at each individual home). Although technically feasible and demonstrated, neighborhood-level
microgrids currently face several logistical, legal, and policy challenges and very few have been developed
in existing communities nation-wide.

However, some policy advancements are currently in development (see the CPUC’s resiliency and
microgrids Rulemaking 19-09-009), and the City’s proposed near term and mid-term actions to facilitate
resilience investments provide an important real option to take further action as soon as barriers to
neighborhood microgrids are cleared or materially reduced.

  25
 City of Beverly Hills: Electrical Resilience Action Plan

Actions to Secure Access to Essential Services in the Event of an Outage
For some residents and businesses, resilience investments may not be feasible, or they may not be
desirable depending on their perception of outage risks and risk tolerances. The City has a critical role in
ensuring that, in an emergency situation, everyone has access to the essential services they need.

  Action (NEAR TERM): Procure additional clean, mobile emergency backup solutions (if
  needed).

These solutions may include backup batteries, solar plus storage-powered trailers, or even diesel
generators, if necessary, that can be delivered to neighborhoods across the city as needed during an
extended outage or in an emergency.

  Action (MID TERM): Develop one or more onsite school microgrids, in partnership
  with the Beverly Hills Unified School District, at a designated emergency shelter such
  as at Hawthorne Elementary School, Horace Mann Elementary School, and/or Beverly
  Vista Middle School.

The school microgrid can serve two critical functions. One, it can ensure the emergency shelter has clean
and continuous power during an emergency. Two, even in blue sky conditions, the microgrid can ensure
students and their families can rely on full school functionality in the event of brief or extended outages.

  Action (MID TERM): Develop one or more onsite City facility microgrids.

As with the school microgrid, a City facility microgrid would improve both onsite resilience in an
emergency situation, and onsite reliability during grid outages. The City facility microgrid will also build
the City’s experience with microgrid planning, design, and operations. The microgrid site should serve
some critical function, be a place where community members can gather during an outage event, and/or
already have energy efficiency upgrades or solar installed for ease of microgrid development. Examples
include the City’s water filtration center, Fire Station #2, Fire Station #3, and the downtown library.

  Action (LONG TERM): Pilot a clustered critical services microgrid.

If the City’s experience with City facility microgrids is positive, this larger-scale microgrid may offer a better
solution than developing microgrids site-by-site. As with the neighborhood-level microgrid pilot, a
clustered critical services microgrid is installed on the distribution system but much closer to the customer
than a substation-level microgrid, and it faces similar barriers. This is also referred to in the industry as a
“town center” microgrid.

  26
 City of Beverly Hills: Electrical Resilience Action Plan

  Action (LONG TERM): Explore targeted public power.

This is an emerging type of municipalization that only serves new grid developments (Wood 2023) and
may be of interest to the City in the future. The City’s experience with operating the City facility and
clustered critical services microgrids will help to determine the feasibility and appetite to plan for and
operate portions of the grid.

CITY OF BEVERLY HILLS
  455 North Rexford Drive
  Beverly Hills, CA 90210
  Video Teleconference
  Mayor’s Citywide Electrical Resilience (MCER) Ad Hoc Committee Meeting

  SPECIAL MEETING HIGHLIGHTS

  Wednesday, January 24, 2024
  3:00 PM

MEETING CALLED TO ORDER
Date / Time:  January 24, 2024 / 3:00 PM
IN ATTENDANCE:  Mayor Julian Gold, Vice Mayor Lester Friedman, Assistant City Manager
  Ryan Gohlich, Public Works Director Shana Epstein, City Consultant
  Mariko Geronimo, Planning Commissioner Jeff Wolfe, Public Works
  Commissioner Homayoon “Mark” Nehoray, Resident-At-Large Ethan
  Bearman, Resident-At-Large Linda Speigel

  1) City of Beverly Hills Electrical Resilience Action Plan:
  a. Added two action items.
  i. improve and ensure that the city has an ongoing data stream for situational
  awareness such as tracking outages, outage causes, and underlying
  hazards on an ongoing basis.
  ii. Increase regulatory pressure on Southern California Edison (SCE).
  b. SCE estimates that the Beverly substation had an hourly peak of 166 megawatts
  in 2023 and will grow by about 3 megawatts per year.
  c. Several strategies were discussed for putting pressure on California Public Utilities
  Commission to pressure SCE such as going to Sacramento to meet with
  lawmakers and forming a united front with several surrounding municipalities.
  d. For residents who want to do something, Geronimo recommends going to the city
  website to see what solutions they can implement on site.
  e. Recommendation that the city get a subscription to PowerOutage.us.
  f. City incentives for solar installations should be considered after the completion of
  resilience audits.
  g. Create a centralized city knowledge guide for residents looking to upgrade to solar
  storage instead of relying on residents to research solar storage options and best
  practices themselves.
  h. The reasoning for why El Rodeo and BHHS were not selected for capacity builds
  was due to their poor locations on the edge of the community rather than a central
  location.
  i. The Waldorf Astoria and Hillton have procured thermal energy storage systems,
  which are hooked up to an HVAC system and creates a backup cooling system
  that is used when daily electricity rates are high.
  j. The current plans for the Resiliency Audit are that it should cover energy efficiency,
  resiliency, what power sources are available, and what other cities have put out in
  terms of energy and resiliency audits.
  k. An RP has been created that would ask to bring on a consultant to conduct the
  audit and create a self-assessment for residents on the city website.
 Highlights for January 24, 2024
Mayor’s Citywide Electrical Resilience (MCER) Ad Hoc Committee

  l. The reason why the action item “Negotiate bulk customer-sited solar and/or energy
  storage purchases for interested residents and small businesses” is mid-term is
  that it requires the resiliency audits to be conducted first and to measure city
  demand for energy storage services.
  m. For the action item “Procure additional clean, mobile emergency backup solutions
  (if needed)” the city would conduct an analysis of the number of diesel backup
  generators they have in their inventory for an emergency. It a gap is found than
  the city will consider clean alternatives to diesel generators such as mobile solar
  plus storage or pre-loaded storage units.
  n. Clean portable generators will have a higher price than diesel generators.
  o. Following the approval and fine tuning of the action plan, the aim is to present it
  before the City Council for approval.
  p. Purchasing the city section of SCE was estimated to cost approximately $700
  million in 2010, which does not account for inflation.
  q. Hydrogen production requires distribution infrastructure and storage and
  downstream infrastructure such as fuel cells, which has not been developed at this
  time, and the technology is in its infancy.
  r. Following refinement of the report, it will be circulated throughout the committee
  members for review, who will meet if they deem it necessary, and if not, the report
  will go directly to the City Council.
  s. Establish an ombudsperson dedicated to electrical resiliency.
  t. One Beverly Hills is still designing their electric system, but they are planning on
  tying into multiple circuits and each tower will have its own backup generator.

  2) Director’s Report:
  a. Staff has created a placeholder city website that has all the electrical resiliency
  resources in one place.

  3) Public Comment:

  None

  Date / Time: January 24, 2024 / 4:02 PM
